title: Modern DevOps: what's trending
intro: In Part 6, Argo CD takes over deploys from git, Prometheus and Grafana show how hello-devops behaves, and your release gets scanned and signed. Then you look at what teams are adopting now: platform engineering, FinOps and AI agents. The last lesson is the capstone, where you ship hello-devops end to end.

lessons.title: GitOps with Argo CD
lessons.goal: By the end you can install Argo CD on your kind cluster, let it deploy hello-devops from your GitHub repo, and fix drift and roll back with nothing but git.

guess.q: With GitOps, how does a new version of your app usually reach the cluster?
options: Your CI pipeline runs kubectl apply with an admin key
A tool inside the cluster pulls the desired state from git
Someone logs in to a server and runs a deploy script
The container registry pushes the new image into the cluster
guess.why: An agent such as Argo CD runs inside the cluster and pulls from git. CI only changes git, so it never needs a key to the cluster.

terms.plain: Running systems from git: the desired state lives in a repo, and an agent keeps the system equal to it.
What you want running, written down as files, here the YAML in your repo.
A difference between what git says and what really runs, often caused by a change made by hand.
A Kubernetes object that tells Argo CD which repo folder to deploy to which cluster and namespace.
Argo CD applying the files from git to the cluster, so the two match.
An Argo CD setting that undoes changes made in the cluster but not in git.
An Argo CD setting that deletes objects from the cluster after you delete them from git.

sections.body:
Until now you deployed with `kubectl apply` from your laptop. That works on day one. Then say a colleague edits a Deployment by hand to fix something late at night. Now git and the cluster disagree, and a week later nobody knows which one is right.

**GitOps** makes git the only place where changes happen. The [OpenGitOps project](https://opengitops.dev/), a CNCF project, puts it in four principles. The desired state must be:
- Declarative: you describe what you want, not the steps to get there.
- Versioned and immutable: it lives in git, with a full history that nobody rewrites.
- Pulled automatically: software agents fetch it from git by themselves.
- Continuously reconciled: agents keep comparing the real system with git and fix differences.

You met the first and the last idea on Day 16. Kubernetes YAML is declarative, and controllers reconcile. GitOps adds git as the source of truth and an agent that watches it.

sections.body:
A new version can reach a cluster in two ways.

With a push deploy, your CI pipeline runs `kubectl apply` or `helm upgrade` against the cluster. So CI needs a key that can write to the cluster, and any workflow that can read that secret can change production.

With a pull deploy, an agent runs inside the cluster. It reads git and applies what it finds. CI builds the image and changes a file in git, and that is all it does. The pull model gives you:
- No cluster keys in CI, because the agent already lives in the cluster.
- An audit log at no extra cost: `git log` shows who changed what, and when.
- Rollback with `git revert`.
- Drift repair: the agent notices hand edits and can undo them.

The price is one more system to run and learn. On a laptop cluster that means a few extra pods. For any cluster that more than one person touches, I think the pull model is worth that price.

Argo CD is a GitOps agent for Kubernetes. It runs as a handful of pods in its own namespace, `argocd`. Three of them do the main work:
- The API server serves the web UI and the `argocd` command line tool.
- The repository server clones your repo and turns a folder into plain YAML. It understands Kustomize and Helm.
- The application controller compares the cluster with that YAML and applies the difference.

You tell Argo CD what to deploy with an Application. It is a custom resource, which means a new object type that a tool adds to Kubernetes. You write it as YAML and apply it like a Deployment. It names a source (repo, branch, folder) and a destination (cluster, namespace).

By default, Argo CD checks git every two to three minutes. A git webhook makes it react within seconds. Every app shows two statuses. Sync status tells you whether the cluster matches git: Synced or OutOfSync. Health tells you whether the objects work, for example Healthy or Progressing. An app can be Synced and still unhealthy, say when a new image crashes on start.

Out of the box, Argo CD only shows you the differences, and you press Sync. Automated sync applies new commits by itself. Two more switches decide how strict it is:
- `selfHeal: true` undoes changes made in the cluster but not in git, such as a `kubectl edit`.
- `prune: true` deletes objects you removed from git. Without it, they stay behind as leftovers.

Both are off by default, a sensible choice for a tool that can delete things. The lab's `argocd/application.yaml` turns both on.

This part trips most people up: other controllers change objects too. Under load, the autoscaler from Day 18 raises the replica count. Argo CD sees a difference from git and, with self-heal on, sets it back. The autoscaler raises it again, and the two fight. The lab file avoids this with `ignoreDifferences` on `/spec/replicas`.

Rollback goes through git as well. You revert the bad commit and push, and Argo CD deploys the old state. Argo CD's own rollback command refuses to run while automated sync is on, because git must stay the source of truth.

sections.h: Getting a new image version into git
sections.body:
Argo CD deploys what git says, and nothing else. So for a new version, something has to write the new image tag into a file and commit it. The usual flow:
1. You push code. CI tests it and builds an image, such as `ghcr.io/you/hello-devops:1.2.0`.
2. A step writes the new tag into `k8s/kustomization.yaml` with `kustomize edit set image`.
3. CI or a person commits that change, often as a pull request.
4. Argo CD sees the new commit and rolls out the new image.

Some teams skip step 2 and run [Argo CD Image Updater](https://github.com/argoproj-labs/argocd-image-updater). It watches the registry and writes new tags back to git, for Kustomize and Helm apps. Its README says it is not yet recommended for critical production workloads, so I would start with the plain flow above.

One catch for the lab: the cluster must be able to pull the image. A new package on GitHub is private by default. For this demo app, make the package public in its settings.

sections.h: Flux, ApplicationSets and app of apps
sections.body:
The other well-known GitOps tool is [Flux](https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2), also a graduated CNCF project. Flux is a set of small controllers that you drive with YAML and the `flux` command, while Argo CD puts a web UI at the center. Both pull from git and reconcile, so what you learn today carries over.

Two Argo CD patterns show up once you have many apps. An ApplicationSet is a template that creates many Applications, for example one per cluster or one per folder in a repo. App of apps is one Application whose folder holds more Application files, so one sync can set up a whole cluster. hello-devops needs neither.

lessons.analogy: Picture a shop with a floor plan pinned up in the back office. The plan says which shelf holds which product. Every few minutes a staff member walks the aisles and puts anything misplaced back where the plan says. If you want the shop to change, you change the plan, and the staff move the products. Where it breaks: a real person would ask why a customer moved something, while Argo CD just puts it back, even when the plan itself is wrong.

steps.say: Say Argo CD already runs on your kind cluster and deploys hello-devops with self-heal on. The task below sets this up. An Application is a normal Kubernetes object, so kubectl can show its two statuses.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n argocd get applications
NAME           SYNC STATUS   HEALTH STATUS
hello-devops   Synced        Healthy

steps.say: Now play the colleague who fixes things by hand. Change the greeting in the live ConfigMap and skip git. A `kubectl scale` would make a poor demo here, because the lab tells Argo CD to ignore replicas.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello patch configmap hello-config --type merge \
    -p '{"data":{"GREETING":"Edited by hand"}}'
configmap/hello-config patched

steps.say: The application controller watches every object it manages, so it sees the change at once and marks the app OutOfSync. Self-heal waits a few seconds (5 by default) and then syncs git's version back.
Check the value. Git's text is back, and you did nothing.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello get configmap hello-config -o jsonpath='{.data.GREETING}'
Hello from Kubernetes!

steps.say: To change the greeting for good, commit it. Edit `k8s/configmap.yaml`, then commit and push. Argo CD applies it at its next check, or right away with `argocd app sync`. Pods read environment variables only when they start, so restart the Deployment to see the new text.
steps.code:
$ git add k8s/configmap.yaml
$ git commit -m "Change the greeting"
$ git push
$ argocd app sync hello-devops
$ kubectl -n hello rollout restart deployment hello-devops

code.title: argocd/application.yaml
code.src:
# An Argo CD Application: "keep the cluster equal to the k8s/ folder in git".
# Apply it once:  kubectl apply -n argocd -f argocd/application.yaml
# Replace <your-github-user> with your GitHub user name first.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  # Applications live in the namespace where Argo CD runs.
  namespace: argocd
  # When you delete this Application, also delete the things it created.
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
spec:
  project: default
  # Where the desired state lives: your repo, branch main, folder k8s.
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/<your-github-user>/hello-devops
    targetRevision: main
    path: k8s
  # Where to deploy: the same cluster Argo CD runs in, namespace hello.
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: hello
  # The autoscaler (k8s/hpa.yaml) changes the number of replicas while the app runs.
  # Ignore that one field, so Argo CD and the autoscaler do not fight.
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      name: hello-devops
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true # delete things that you removed from git
      selfHeal: true # undo changes made by hand in the cluster
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true # create namespace hello if it is missing
      - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true # also skip /spec/replicas when syncing

commands.what: Create the namespace where Argo CD runs.
Install Argo CD from its official manifest. Server-side apply is needed because some of its definitions are very large.
Check that all Argo CD pods are Running.
Open the Argo CD UI at https://localhost:8443 and accept the self-signed certificate warning.
Install the argocd command line tool on your Mac.
Print the first password of the admin user.
Log the CLI in through the port-forward. --insecure accepts the self-signed certificate.
List Applications with their sync and health status.
Show one app: repo, path, status and every object it manages.
Sync now instead of waiting for the next check of git.
Run inside k8s/ (install with brew install kustomize). Writes a new image name and tag into kustomization.yaml.
Make a new commit that undoes the last one. Push it, and Argo CD rolls back.

lessons.mistake: Fixing something in the cluster by hand and expecting the fix to stay. With self-heal on, Argo CD undoes `kubectl edit` and `kubectl delete` within seconds. Make the change in git and let Argo CD apply it. In a real emergency, turn off automated sync for that app first, and write down what you changed so it reaches git afterwards.
lessons.real_world: A payments team might keep one config repo with a folder per environment: dev, staging and prod. Merging a pull request into the prod folder is the deploy, and the review is the approval. When a release breaks at night, the on-call engineer reverts the commit. Argo CD rolls back, and git records who did what.

task.title: Put hello-devops under GitOps
steps: Start your kind cluster from Day 16 if it is not running, and make sure your latest `k8s/` folder is pushed to GitHub.
Install Argo CD with the first two commands in the Commands list. Wait until every pod in namespace `argocd` is Running.
Open the UI with a port-forward and log in as `admin` with the initial password.
Add `argocd/application.yaml` to your repo with your GitHub user name in `repoURL`. Commit, push, and apply it.
Watch the app in the UI until it shows Synced and Healthy. Click it and look at the tree of objects.
Remove `hpa.yaml` from the `resources` list in `k8s/kustomization.yaml`, then commit and push. Watch prune delete the HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
Undo that with `git revert HEAD` and push. Watch the HorizontalPodAutoscaler come back.
hints: If the app shows a repository error, Argo CD cannot read your repo. A public repo needs no password; for a private one, run `argocd repo add` with a read-only token.
Argo CD checks git every few minutes. Press Refresh in the UI, or run `argocd app sync hello-devops`, to skip the wait.
task.done_when: After your revert, `kubectl -n hello get hpa` lists hello-devops again, and Argo CD shows the app as Synced and Healthy.

explain_back.prompt: Explain GitOps to a teammate in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention who applies changes, what self-heal does, and how you roll back.
explain_back.answer: With GitOps, git holds the desired state of the cluster, and an agent inside the cluster applies it. Nobody runs kubectl apply by hand; a change is a commit, usually through a pull request. Argo CD keeps comparing the cluster with git, and self-heal undoes changes that skipped git. To roll back, you revert the commit, and Argo CD deploys the old state.

recap: GitOps: git holds the desired state, and an agent in the cluster pulls it and keeps the cluster equal to it.
Pull deploys keep cluster keys out of CI, and git gives you the audit log and the rollback.
An Argo CD Application links a repo folder to a cluster and a namespace.
Automated sync applies new commits, self-heal undoes hand edits, and prune deletes what you removed from git.
Tell Argo CD to ignore fields that other controllers own, such as replicas set by an autoscaler.
A new version ships when CI changes the image tag in git, for example with kustomize edit set image.

check.q: A teammate scales hello-devops to 10 pods with kubectl. Your Application has selfHeal on and ignores /spec/replicas. What does Argo CD do?
options: It sets the count back to 3 within seconds
It leaves it alone; only the autoscaler may change it
It deletes the Deployment and creates it again
It marks the app Degraded and stops syncing
check.why: ignoreDifferences tells Argo CD not to compare /spec/replicas, so this is not drift to it. The autoscaler still applies its own maximum of 6.

check.q: You delete redis.yaml from git and push. Automated sync is on, but prune is off. What happens to Redis in the cluster?
options: It is deleted at the next sync
Argo CD puts redis.yaml back into your repo
It keeps running, and Argo CD flags it as needing a prune
The sync fails and nothing else deploys
check.why: Without prune, automated sync never deletes anything. The object stays, marked as no longer in git, until you prune it.

check.q: Your CI pipeline holds a cluster admin key and runs kubectl apply after every build. What is the main GitOps improvement?
options: CI only updates the tag in git, and Argo CD applies it
CI runs kubectl apply twice to be sure it worked
Developers apply from their laptops instead of CI
The cluster pulls images from Docker Hub, not GHCR
check.why: Moving the apply into the cluster takes the powerful key away from CI, and git becomes the record of every deploy.

interview.q: What is GitOps, and how is it different from a CI pipeline that runs kubectl apply?
interview.a: GitOps keeps the desired state of a system in git, and an agent such as Argo CD or Flux pulls it and keeps the system equal to it. A push pipeline runs kubectl apply from outside, so it needs cluster credentials and only acts when it runs. The GitOps agent runs inside the cluster, keeps reconciling, and can undo drift. Every change is a commit, so review, history and rollback come from normal git tools.

interview.q: How do you roll back a bad deploy in an Argo CD setup?
interview.a: I revert the commit that introduced the change and push, so git again describes the last good state. Argo CD syncs and the cluster follows. Argo CD has its own rollback command, but it cannot run while automated sync is on, and it would leave the cluster different from git. A git revert keeps one source of truth and leaves an audit trail.

deeper.body:
Once CI writes to git, you have two design choices: which repo holds the YAML, and who writes the tag.

With one repo, code and YAML live together, as in hello-devops. It is simple. The downside is that every tag bump becomes a commit in the code history. CI must also not trigger itself: a commit that only changes `k8s/` should not build a new image. A paths filter on the workflow (Day 11) handles that.

With two repos, the app repo holds code and a config repo holds the YAML for every environment. CI in the app repo builds the image, then opens a pull request in the config repo. Teams pick this when:
- Many people may change code, but only a few may change production.
- They want the config history to read like a deploy log.
- One config repo describes many apps and clusters.

For one person and one laptop cluster, one repo is plenty. Who writes the tag? From manual to automatic:
1. A person edits the tag in a pull request. Slow, but very clear.
2. CI runs `kustomize edit set image` (or edits Helm values) and opens a pull request with a narrow token.
3. Argo CD Image Updater watches the registry and writes the tag itself, for example "the newest 1.x version".

Promotion between environments works the same way. To move version 1.2.0 from staging to prod, you copy the tag from one folder to the other in a pull request. The image is built once and promoted by changing text, which is the "build once, deploy many" idea from Day 9.

When it really matters, pin by digest. Someone can push a tag such as `1.2.0` again by mistake, but a digest such as `@sha256:...` always means the same bytes. The `images` field in `kustomization.yaml` accepts a `digest` value for this.

lessons.title: Observability: metrics, logs and traces
lessons.goal: By the end you can install Prometheus and Grafana on kind, scrape hello-devops with a ServiceMonitor, write a basic PromQL query, and explain logs, traces and SLOs.

guess.q: How does Prometheus usually get metrics from your app?
options: Your app sends each number to Prometheus as it happens
Grafana collects the numbers and stores them for Prometheus
Prometheus calls the app's /metrics page every few seconds
Kubernetes saves app metrics in etcd for Prometheus to read
guess.why: Prometheus pulls: it scrapes a page such as /metrics on a schedule. Grafana only draws charts from the data Prometheus stores.

terms.plain: How well you can understand what a system is doing inside by looking at what it outputs.
A number measured over time, such as requests per second or memory in use.
Prometheus fetching the current metric values from a target's /metrics page.
A metric that only goes up (or drops to zero on restart), such as total requests served.
The path of one request through all the services it touches, made of timed steps called spans.
Service level objective: a target for how good a service must be, such as 99.9% of requests succeed.
The amount of failure an SLO allows, such as 0.1% of requests over 30 days.

sections.body:
Monitoring means watching for problems you already know about. Is the pod up? Is the disk full? You write a check and an alert for each one.

**Observability** is how well you can answer new questions about a running system from what it outputs, without shipping new code. Here is an observability question: why are requests from one country slow since 14:00? No check you wrote last month answers that. Systems give you four kinds of signals:
- Metrics: numbers over time. Cheap to store, good for graphs and alerts.
- Logs: lines of text about single events, such as one failed request.
- Traces: the path of one request through many services, with timings.
- Profiles: where the code spends CPU and memory. The newest signal; OpenTelemetry support is still alpha.

In practice, a metric alert tells you something is wrong. Then you open logs and traces to find where, and why.

sections.body:
Prometheus is the standard metrics system on Kubernetes, and it pulls. Every few seconds it scrapes each target: it calls a page such as `/metrics` and stores the numbers with a timestamp. Your app already serves this page. Each line is one time series: a name, some labels (key and value pairs), and a value:

`hello_requests_total{path="/"} 90.0`

You will meet three metric types:
- Counter: only goes up, like `hello_requests_total`.
- Gauge: goes up and down, like memory in use or the length of a queue.
- Histogram: counts values in buckets, such as how many requests took under 100 ms. You use it for latency.

You ask questions in PromQL, the Prometheus query language. A raw counter only grows, so you almost always want its speed instead. `rate(hello_requests_total[5m])` gives requests per second, averaged over the last 5 minutes, and `sum(rate(hello_requests_total[5m]))` adds up all pods. If you learn one PromQL function, make it `rate()`. Grafana runs queries like these and draws the results as dashboards.

On Kubernetes you rarely install Prometheus by hand. The kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart installs the whole set at once:
- Prometheus, to scrape and store metrics.
- Grafana, with ready-made dashboards for the cluster.
- Alertmanager, to send alerts to email or chat.
- The Prometheus Operator, which runs Prometheus and Alertmanager for you.
- Exporters that publish metrics about nodes and Kubernetes objects.

An operator is a controller that runs a piece of software for you, driven by custom resources. The custom resource you need here is the ServiceMonitor. It says: find Services with these labels, then scrape this port and path. The operator turns it into Prometheus settings.

This trips most people up. By default, this Prometheus only reads ServiceMonitors that carry the label `release` with the Helm release name. The lab installs the chart as `monitoring`, so `observability/servicemonitor.yaml` has `release: monitoring`. Leave the label out and nothing fails. Your app just never shows up, and you get no error to search for.

sections.h: Logs: write to stdout, ship with an agent
sections.body:
In a container, your app should write logs to standard output (stdout), one event per line, and leave log files alone. Kubernetes keeps each container's output on the node, and `kubectl logs` reads it.

That works for one pod and the last few minutes. It falls apart with 30 pods on 3 nodes, or with a pod that was deleted an hour ago. So teams add a log pipeline:
1. An agent runs on every node, for example Grafana Alloy or Fluent Bit.
2. It reads the container logs, adds labels such as namespace and pod, and sends them on.
3. A log store keeps them. [Loki](https://grafana.com/docs/loki/latest/get-started/overview/) is a common choice next to Prometheus.
4. You search them in Grafana with LogQL, a query language that looks like PromQL.

Loki indexes only the labels, not the full text, which keeps storage cheap. Write logs as JSON when you can, so fields such as `status` and `path` are easy to filter.

A trace follows one request. Say a checkout call goes through an API, a payment service and a database. The trace shows each step as a span, with its start time and duration. One look tells you that most of the time went into waiting for the database.

To get traces, code must create spans and pass a trace ID along with each call. [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/what-is-opentelemetry/), often called OTel, is the open standard for this. It is a CNCF project, and it gives you:
- APIs and SDKs for many languages, including Python and Java.
- Automatic instrumentation for common libraries, so you write less code.
- OTLP, one protocol for traces, metrics and logs.
- The Collector, a service that receives telemetry, processes it (for example, batching or filtering) and exports it.

OpenTelemetry is vendor neutral, and it stores nothing itself. You send its data to a backend such as Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Prometheus or a paid service, and you can switch backends without touching your code.

refs.title: OpenTelemetry: what it is and is not

sections.body:
What should you measure first? [Google's SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/) names four golden signals:
- Latency: how long requests take.
- Traffic: how many requests arrive.
- Errors: how many requests fail.
- Saturation: how full the system is, such as CPU or memory.

For a single service, the [RED method](https://grafana.com/blog/the-red-method-how-to-instrument-your-services/) keeps the user-facing ones: rate, errors and duration.

Then decide what good means. An SLI (service level indicator) is a measurement, such as the share of requests that succeed. An SLO is the target for it, such as 99.9% over 30 days. What is left over is the error budget. A 99.9% target allows about 43 minutes of full downtime in 30 days. While budget remains, ship at normal speed. When it runs out, reliability work comes first.

Alert on symptoms users feel, such as many errors or slow responses. High CPU on its own should not wake anyone up. After an incident, the team writes a blameless postmortem: what happened and how to prevent it, with no person to blame.

lessons.analogy: A car gives you three views of a drive. The dashboard gauges are metrics: speed and fuel, always on and quick to read. The trip log is like logs, with one line for each stop. A GPS replay of one drive is a trace: every turn, and how long each part took. Where it breaks: a car has one driver, while your app serves thousands of requests at once. So you have to choose what to record and how long to keep it.

steps.say: Two containers are enough to see the whole pull model. Start the app with a single gunicorn worker. With two workers, each keeps its own counter, and Go deeper explains why that confuses Prometheus.
steps.code:
$ docker network create obs
$ docker run -d --name hello --network obs -p 8000:8000 hello-devops:1.0.0 \
    gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 1 --no-control-socket app:app

steps.say: Tell Prometheus what to scrape. Save this as `prometheus.yml` in an empty folder. On Kubernetes, a ServiceMonitor generates settings like these for you.
steps.code:
# prometheus.yml: scrape the container named "hello" every 5 seconds.
global:
  scrape_interval: 5s
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: hello
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["hello:8000"]

steps.say: Run Prometheus from Docker Hub with your file mounted. It finds the app by its container name on the shared network (Day 7).
steps.code:
$ docker run -d --name prom --network obs -p 9090:9090 \
    -v "$PWD/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml" prom/prometheus

steps.say: Send 60 requests, one per second, so there is something to measure.
steps.code: $ for i in $(seq 1 60); do curl -s localhost:8000/ > /dev/null; sleep 1; done

steps.say: Ask for the raw counter through the HTTP API. The web UI at http://localhost:9090 shows the same thing. I had sent 30 requests before this, so mine says 90. Prometheus added the `job` and `instance` labels itself.
steps.code:
$ curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=hello_requests_total'
{"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{"__name__":"hello_requests_total","instance":"hello:8000","job":"hello","path":"/"},"value":[1793331673.198,"90"]}]}}

steps.say: Now ask for the speed. `rate(...[1m])` is the increase per second over the last minute. It comes out at about 1, because you sent one request per second.
steps.code:
$ curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=rate(hello_requests_total[1m])'
{"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{"instance":"hello:8000","job":"hello","path":"/"},"value":[1793331673.187,"1.0000000000000002"]}]}}

steps.code:
$ docker rm -f hello prom
$ docker network rm obs

code.src:
# Settings for the kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart on a laptop kind cluster.
# It installs Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager and the Prometheus Operator.
#
# Install (check the chart's README for the current command):
#   helm install monitoring oci://ghcr.io/prometheus-community/charts/kube-prometheus-stack \
#     --namespace monitoring --create-namespace -f observability/values.yaml
#
# The release name "monitoring" matters. By default, this Prometheus only reads
# ServiceMonitors that carry the label release: monitoring.

# On kind, these control plane parts listen only on 127.0.0.1 inside their node,
# so Prometheus cannot reach them. Skip them to avoid false "down" targets.
kubeControllerManager:
  enabled: false
kubeScheduler:
  enabled: false
kubeEtcd:
  enabled: false
kubeProxy:
  enabled: false

prometheus:
  prometheusSpec:
    # Keep one day of data. This is a lab, not production.
    retention: 1d

grafana:
  # Show times in your browser's time zone.
  defaultDashboardsTimezone: browser

code.title: observability/servicemonitor.yaml
code.src:
# Tells Prometheus to scrape hello-devops every 15 seconds.
# Needs kube-prometheus-stack (see values.yaml). It finds the Service in
# k8s/service.yaml by its label app: hello-devops and its port named http.
# Apply: kubectl apply -f observability/servicemonitor.yaml
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello
  labels:
    # Prometheus from the "monitoring" Helm release only reads
    # ServiceMonitors with this label.
    release: monitoring
spec:
  # Find Services with this label ...
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-devops
  # ... in this namespace.
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames:
      - hello
  endpoints:
    - port: http # the name of the Service port (port 80, which leads to 8000)
      path: /metrics
      interval: 15s

task.title: Watch hello-devops in Grafana
steps: Make sure your kind cluster runs and hello-devops is deployed, by Argo CD (Day 20) or with kubectl.
Add `observability/values.yaml` to your repo and install kube-prometheus-stack with Helm as the release `monitoring`.
Check that `k8s/service.yaml` has the label `app: hello-devops` and a port named `http`, then apply `observability/servicemonitor.yaml`.
Port-forward Prometheus and confirm that three hello-devops targets are up.
Port-forward Grafana, read the admin password from its Secret, and log in.
In Grafana, open Explore, choose the Prometheus data source, and run `sum(rate(hello_requests_total[5m]))`.
Send traffic with a curl loop against http://localhost:8081 and watch the line rise. Save the query as a panel on a new dashboard.
hints: No target? The labels do not match. Compare the ServiceMonitor with `kubectl -n hello get svc --show-labels`, and check its `release` label.
rate() needs at least two scrapes inside its window. Wait a minute after the first traffic.
If pods stay Pending, Docker Desktop is short of memory. Give it more under Settings, then Resources.
task.done_when: Your Grafana panel shows `sum(rate(hello_requests_total[5m]))` rising while your curl loop runs.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate how hello-devops metrics end up in a Grafana chart, in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention scrape, ServiceMonitor and PromQL.
explain_back.answer: The app serves its counters on /metrics. Prometheus scrapes that page every 15 seconds and stores each value with a timestamp. It knows where to look because the Prometheus Operator turns our ServiceMonitor, which matches the hello-devops Service by label, into scrape settings. Grafana runs a PromQL query such as sum(rate(hello_requests_total[5m])) and draws the result.

recap: Monitoring watches for known problems; observability lets you ask new questions from a system's outputs.
Metrics say that something is wrong; logs and traces help you find where and why. Profiles are a newer, fourth signal.
Prometheus pulls: it scrapes /metrics on a schedule and stores time series with labels.
Use rate() on counters to get per-second speed, and let Grafana draw PromQL results.
A ServiceMonitor tells the Prometheus Operator what to scrape, and it needs the release label.
Set SLOs on what users feel, alert on symptoms, and write blameless postmortems after incidents.

check.q: You want a graph of how many requests per second hello-devops serves. Which query fits?
options: hello_requests_total
rate(hello_requests_total[5m])
max(hello_requests_total)
count(hello_requests_total)
check.why: A counter only grows; rate() turns it into speed per second over the window.

check.q: Your new ServiceMonitor applies without errors, but Prometheus shows no hello-devops target. What do you check first?
options: Whether Grafana has the right data source
Whether the app writes its logs to stdout
Whether the pods have enough CPU requests
Whether its labels and selector match the release and the Service
check.why: Prometheus only reads ServiceMonitors with the release label, and the selector must match the Service's labels. A mismatch fails without any error.

check.q: Your SLO is 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. Halfway through the month, 0.08% of requests have failed. What does this tell you?
options: Most of the error budget is gone, so slow down risky changes
The SLO is met, so you can stop measuring for now
The error budget is still untouched
You should alert on CPU instead of errors
check.why: The budget is 0.1%. With 0.08% already used and half the month left, reliability work comes first.

interview.q: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
interview.a: Monitoring watches for known failures with checks and alerts, such as a pod being down or a disk filling up. Observability is how well you can understand a system's inner state from its outputs, including questions you did not plan for. In practice it comes from good metrics, structured logs and traces that share labels and IDs. Monitoring tells you that something is wrong; observability helps you find out why.

interview.q: What are SLOs and error budgets, and how do they change how a team works?
interview.a: An SLI measures service quality, like the share of successful requests, and an SLO is the target for it over a time window, like 99.9% over 30 days. The error budget is what the SLO allows to fail, here 0.1%. While the budget lasts, the team ships features at normal speed; when it is spent, effort moves to reliability. Alerts then fire on fast budget burn instead of on raw CPU or memory.

deeper.body:
Our image runs gunicorn with two worker processes. Each worker is a separate Python process with its own copy of `hello_requests_total`. When Prometheus scrapes `/metrics`, gunicorn hands the request to one worker, and you only see that worker's number. Try it: send 6 requests, then fetch `/metrics` a few times. I saw 5, then 1, then 5 again.

Prometheus sees a counter that went down and treats it as a restart. `rate()` then counts the jumps as new requests, so the speed looks higher than it is. That is why the worked example ran one worker. Real apps fix this in one of two ways:
- Run one worker per container and add more pods. Kubernetes already handles the scaling.
- Use the Python client's multiprocess mode: workers share a folder set by `PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR`, and `/metrics` adds them up.

A counter tells you how many requests you served, not how fast. For speed you need a histogram. It counts requests into buckets: under 0.1 seconds, under 0.25 seconds, and so on. In Python you would add `Histogram("hello_request_seconds", "Request time")` and time the handler with it. PromQL can then estimate a percentile:

`histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(hello_request_seconds_bucket[5m])))`

This reads: the time within which 95% of requests finished, over the last 5 minutes. I trust percentiles more than averages. If 99 requests take 10 ms and one takes 5 seconds, the average looks fine, but one user waited 5 seconds.

Alerts come last. An alerting rule is a PromQL expression plus a duration. For example, fire when more than 5% of requests fail for 10 minutes. kube-prometheus-stack reads rules from PrometheusRule objects, found by the same `release` label as ServiceMonitors. Alertmanager groups the alerts and sends them to chat, email or a paging tool.

lessons.goal: By the end you can scan, list and sign the hello-devops image in CI, verify its signature and provenance, and block risky Pods with a Kyverno policy.

guess.q: Your workflow uses a popular action as some-org/some-action@v4. An attacker steals the maintainer's token. What can happen on your next run?
options: Nothing, because a version tag can never point to new code
GitHub scans the action and blocks the run for you
Only forks of your repo would run the bad code
Your run executes the attacker's code, because tags can move
guess.why: A git tag is a pointer that can be moved. In the 2025 tj-actions/changed-files attack, tags were moved to a malicious commit; pinning to a full commit SHA prevents this.

terms.plain: An attack on something you depend on (a library, a tool, a build step) instead of on your own code.
Software bill of materials: a list of every package and version inside an artifact, like an ingredient label.
A public ID for one known security bug, such as CVE-2024-3094.
Signing with a short-lived certificate tied to an identity, such as a CI workflow, so there is no long-lived private key.
A signed record of how, where and from which source an artifact was built.
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: a framework that grades how trustworthy a build is, in levels.
A rule the Kubernetes API checks before it stores an object, used to block risky settings.

sections.h: Shift left: security as part of the pipeline
sections.body:
In many companies, a security team used to look at a release once, near the end. DevSecOps moves that work into the daily routine of everyone who writes and ships code.

Shift left means moving checks earlier, to the left side of the pipeline drawing. A leaked password caught before `git push` costs you a minute. The same leak found in production can cost a weekend of rotating keys. So you put cheap, automatic checks where code is written and built:
- Secret scanning before the push and on every commit.
- Dependency and image scanning in CI.
- Signing and provenance at release time.
- Policies when objects enter the cluster.

The other big idea is least privilege: every person, token and pod gets only the rights it needs, for only as long as it needs them. You have done this three times already: the `permissions` block (Day 12), OIDC instead of stored cloud keys (Day 15), and a non-root user in the Dockerfile (Day 8).

refs.title: GitHub Docs: security hardening for GitHub Actions

sections.body:
Attackers often skip your code and go after something you trust. Three recent cases:
- xz-utils (2024): a trusted maintainer account hid a backdoor in the release files of a compression library.
- tj-actions/changed-files (March 2025): attackers moved an action's version tags to code that printed CI secrets into logs.
- Trivy (March 2026): with stolen credentials, attackers force-pushed 76 of 77 `trivy-action` tags and shipped a malicious release.

The xz backdoor could reach the SSH server on some Linux systems. A developer, Andres Freund, noticed SSH logins using too much CPU and traced the cause to xz. GitHub's advisory on tj-actions says over 23,000 repositories used that action. And Trivy is the scanner you add to your pipeline today.

The defenses are simple habits. Pin actions to a full commit SHA, verify what you download, keep CI tokens narrow, and rotate secrets after an incident. That is why the new `release.yml` pins `trivy-action` to a commit, not a tag.

sections.h: Know what is inside: SBOMs and scanning
sections.body:
Your image holds about 100 packages: Debian packages from the base image, Python itself, and your app's libraries. You wrote none of them. An SBOM (software bill of materials) lists them all with their versions. The two standard formats are SPDX and CycloneDX, and the tool `syft` writes either one. When the next big bug is announced, you search your SBOMs instead of guessing which images are affected.

A vulnerability scanner compares those packages with public lists of known bugs. Each bug has a CVE ID. Trivy scans images with `trivy image`. With `trivy config`, it checks files such as Dockerfiles, Kubernetes YAML and Terraform for risky settings.

Scanners report a lot, so decide up front what stops the pipeline. A rule I like: fail on HIGH and CRITICAL issues that already have a fixed version, and track the rest. Failing on every LOW finding mostly teaches people to ignore the scanner.

Secrets need their own scanner. GitHub push protection blocks known secret formats when you push. For your own account it is on by default for public repos. On your laptop, `gitleaks git` scans your whole git history.

A scan tells you what is inside. A signature tells you who made it, and that nobody changed it since. With **keyless signing** from cosign (part of the Sigstore project), you never store a private key:
1. The release job asks GitHub for an OIDC token that says "this is release.yml in this repo, on tag v1.2.0".
2. Fulcio, Sigstore's certificate authority, trades it for a certificate that is valid for about ten minutes.
3. cosign signs the image digest and stores the signature in the registry, next to the image.
4. The signing event goes into Rekor, a public log that nobody can quietly edit.

Later, anyone can run `cosign verify` and demand that exact workflow identity.

Provenance goes one step further. It is a signed statement of how the image was built: which repo, which commit, which workflow. SLSA (say "salsa") grades builds in levels. Level 1 means provenance exists. At Level 2, a hosted build platform creates and signs it. Level 3 adds a build platform hardened against tampering. GitHub artifact attestations give you Build Level 2, and building inside a shared reusable workflow can reach Level 3.

refs.title: GitHub Docs: artifact attestations for build provenance

sections.h: Policy as code at the cluster door
sections.body:
CI checks only cover images that go through CI. Anyone with access can still run `kubectl run` with any image. So you also check at the cluster door.

Before the Kubernetes API server stores an object, it can ask admission webhooks whether to accept it. A policy engine answers. Its rules are code, and you keep them in git. The two common engines:
- Kyverno: policies are Kubernetes YAML, with checks written in CEL, a short expression language that Kubernetes also uses.
- OPA Gatekeeper: policies are written in Rego, a general policy language.

For a Kubernetes-only shop I would pick Kyverno, because the policies look like the YAML you already write. The lab's `policy/` folder has two Kyverno policies. One rejects images tagged `:latest` or with no tag at all. The other reports Pods that do not set `runAsNonRoot: true`.

Each policy has a mode. Audit allows the object but records a failure in a PolicyReport. Deny blocks it. Roll out a new rule in Audit, fix what it finds, then switch to Deny. In Kyverno 1.19 the older ClusterPolicy type is deprecated, with removal planned for 1.20, so the lab uses the newer ValidatingPolicy type.

lessons.analogy: Think of packaged food. The ingredient label is the SBOM, and the safety inspection is the vulnerability scan. A tamper-evident seal with the factory's stamp is the signature, and the farm-to-shelf record is the provenance. The shop's rule "no product without a seal" is the admission policy. Where it breaks: a seal proves who packed the food and that nobody opened it. It says nothing about whether the food is good, and a signed image can still contain a bug.

worked.title: Triage a scan of your own image

steps.say: Install the tools with Homebrew. syft writes SBOMs and trivy scans for known bugs. Both read images straight from Docker Desktop.
steps.code: $ brew install syft trivy

steps.say: Write an SBOM of the image you built on Day 8, then look for your main packages. The full list has about 100 entries, and most of them come from Debian.
steps.code:
$ syft hello-devops:1.0.0 -o spdx-json=sbom.spdx.json
$ syft hello-devops:1.0.0 -q | grep -E '^(NAME|flask|gunicorn|redis) '
NAME                     VERSION                            TYPE
flask                    3.1.3                              python
gunicorn                 26.2.0                             python
redis                    8.1.0                              python

steps.say: Scan it, and show only HIGH and CRITICAL issues that have a fix. My run on 30 October 2026 found 5, all in one group (trimmed).
steps.code:
$ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed hello-devops:1.0.0
...
Python (python-pkg)
===================
Total: 5 (HIGH: 5, CRITICAL: 0)

│ msgpack    │ CVE-2026-114613     │ HIGH     │ fixed  │ 1.1.2             │ 1.2.3
│            │ GHSA-6v7p-g79w-8964 │          │        │                   │ 1.2.1
│ setuptools │ CVE-2025-47273      │          │        │ 70.3.0            │ 78.1.1
│ urllib3    │ CVE-2026-97687      │          │        │ 2.7.0             │ 2.8.0
│            │ CVE-2026-97689      │          │        │                   │

steps.say: Read the names before you fix anything. msgpack, setuptools and urllib3 are not in your requirements.txt. Instead, pip, the installer, carries its own copies of them. The app needs pip to install packages, not to run. So the fix is to remove pip from the final image.

Add the two `pip uninstall` lines from the Dockerfile in Files, rebuild as 1.2.0, and scan again. The flag `--exit-code 1` makes trivy fail the shell on a finding, the same way it fails CI. Exit code 0 means clean.
steps.code:
$ docker build -t hello-devops:1.2.0 --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.2.0 .
$ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 hello-devops:1.2.0
...
$ echo $?
0

steps.say: New CVEs appear every day, so your numbers will differ. When a scan fails, first update: a newer base image or package. Next, remove what you do not need. Only then accept the risk in a `.trivyignore` file, with a reason and a date to look again.

code.title: .github/workflows/release.yml (Day 22: scan, SBOM, sign, attest)
code.src:
name: release

# Runs when you push a version tag such as v1.2.0.
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

# Default for every job: the GITHUB_TOKEN can only read the repository.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  image:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    # Approval gate: add required reviewers to "production" in
    # Settings > Environments. Without rules, the job just runs.
    environment: production
    # This job alone gets more rights, and only the ones it needs.
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write # push images to GHCR
      id-token: write # ask GitHub for an OIDC token, used for keyless signing (Day 22)
      attestations: write # store provenance and SBOM attestations (Day 22)
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Third-party actions are pinned to a full commit SHA.
      # The comment shows the version. Dependabot keeps both up to date.
      - name: Set up QEMU (to build arm64 on an amd64 runner)
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@99012661954931238ded8c8b007157a8430204e1 # v4.4.0
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@f87e5991a6d7451dcb8d9637bfbc97413f497069 # v4.4.1

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@81c6f93d4bc991e510b342a00b419b3bb4efc5c6 # v4.7.0
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Registries need lower case names, and a GitHub user name may have capitals.
      - name: Set the image name
        run: echo "IMAGE=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Work out image tags and labels
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@dc802804100637a589fabce1cb79ff13a1411302 # v6.2.0
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}
          # Tag v1.2.0 gives 1.2.0, sha-<short commit> and latest.
          tags: |
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
            type=sha

      # Day 22, step 1: build for this runner only and load the image into
      # the local Docker engine. Nothing is pushed yet.
      - name: Build the image for scanning
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          load: true
          tags: hello-devops:scan
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          cache-from: type=gha

      # Day 22, step 2: stop the release on HIGH or CRITICAL issues that have a fix.
      - name: Scan the image with Trivy
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0
        with:
          image-ref: hello-devops:scan
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          ignore-unfixed: true
          exit-code: "1"

      - name: Build and push (amd64 and arm64)
        id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          # The app reports this version at "/" (1.2.0 for tag v1.2.0).
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

      # Day 22, step 3: write the ingredient list (SBOM) of the pushed image.
      - name: Create an SBOM (SPDX format)
        uses: anchore/sbom-action@66cbf4bc1f1c0d2edc94016e65bc221b6bb0ad6c # v0.24.3
        with:
          image: ${{ env.IMAGE }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          format: spdx-json
          output-file: sbom.spdx.json

      # Day 22, step 4: sign the image by its digest. Keyless: no private key to
      # store or leak. The signature is tied to this workflow's identity.
      - name: Install cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@6f9f17788090df1f26f669e9d70d6ae9567deba6 # v4.1.2
      - name: Sign the image
        env:
          DIGEST: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
        run: cosign sign --yes "${IMAGE}@${DIGEST}"

      # Day 22, step 5: record how the image was built (SLSA provenance) and
      # attach the SBOM. Free for public repositories. Storage records only
      # work for repositories owned by an organization, so they are off here.
      - name: Attest build provenance
        uses: actions/attest@v4
        with:
          subject-name: ${{ env.IMAGE }}
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          push-to-registry: true
          create-storage-record: false
      - name: Attest the SBOM
        uses: actions/attest@v4
        with:
          subject-name: ${{ env.IMAGE }}
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          sbom-path: sbom.spdx.json
          push-to-registry: true
          create-storage-record: false

      - name: Show the image digest in the run summary
        env:
          DIGEST: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          TAGS: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
        run: |
          {
            echo "### Pushed and signed image"
            echo "Digest: \`$DIGEST\`"
            echo '```'
            echo "$TAGS"
            echo '```'
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---- build stage: install dependencies into a virtual environment ----
FROM python:3.14-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
RUN python -m venv /venv
ENV PATH="/venv/bin:$PATH"
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
# pip is only needed to install packages. Remove it from the venv we ship.
RUN pip uninstall -y pip

# ---- run stage: only what the app needs at run time ----
FROM python:3.14-slim
# The base image has its own pip. The app does not need it, so remove it too.
RUN pip uninstall -y pip
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /venv /venv
ENV PATH="/venv/bin:$PATH" PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
COPY app.py .
# The version is baked in at build time: docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.2.0 .
ARG APP_VERSION=dev
ENV APP_VERSION=$APP_VERSION
# Run as a normal user, not root.
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --no-create-home appuser
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/healthz')"
# --no-control-socket: Gunicorn 26 would otherwise try to open a socket in a home folder this user does not have.
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "2", "--no-control-socket", "app:app"]

# Kyverno policy: every container image needs a fixed tag, and never :latest.
# Apply: kubectl apply -f policy/disallow-latest-tag.yaml
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: ValidatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: disallow-latest-tag
spec:
  # Deny = block the request. Audit = allow it, but record a failure in a report.
  validationActions:
    - Deny
  # Check Pods only in namespace hello, our app's namespace.
  matchConstraints:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: hello
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [pods]
  # Also check Deployments, so a bad Deployment fails at kubectl apply time.
  autogen:
    podControllers:
      controllers:
        - deployments
  validations:
    # The part after the last "/" must contain ":" (a tag) or the image uses "@" (a digest).
    - expression: >-
        object.spec.containers.all(c,
        c.image.substring(c.image.lastIndexOf('/') + 1).contains(':') || c.image.contains('@'))
      message: "Every image needs a tag, for example hello-devops:1.0.0."
    - expression: "object.spec.containers.all(c, !c.image.endsWith(':latest'))"
      message: "The :latest tag is not allowed. Use a fixed version tag."

# Kyverno policy: Pods must promise to run as a non-root user.
# It starts in Audit mode: nothing is blocked, failures show up in a PolicyReport.
# Apply: kubectl apply -f policy/require-run-as-nonroot.yaml
# Read:  kubectl get policyreport -n hello
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: ValidatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-run-as-nonroot
spec:
  validationActions:
    - Audit
  # Also check Pods that already exist, not only new ones.
  evaluation:
    background:
      enabled: true
  matchConstraints:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: hello
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [pods]
  autogen:
    podControllers:
      controllers:
        - deployments
  validations:
    # Pass when the Pod sets runAsNonRoot: true, or every container does.
    - expression: >-
        object.spec.?securityContext.?runAsNonRoot.orValue(false) ||
        object.spec.containers.all(c, c.?securityContext.?runAsNonRoot.orValue(false))
      message: "Set securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true on the Pod or on every container."

task.title: Ship a signed release and guard the cluster
steps: Update your `Dockerfile` and `.github/workflows/release.yml` to the versions in Files. Build locally and check that trivy passes with `--exit-code 1`.
Commit and push, then tag `v1.2.0` and push the tag. Watch the release run in the Actions tab.
Make the hello-devops package public in its package settings on GitHub, so your kind cluster can pull it later.
Verify the signature with `cosign verify` and the provenance with `gh attestation verify`.
Install Kyverno with Helm, then apply both files from `policy/`.
Run `kubectl -n hello run test --image=nginx:latest` and read the rejection message.
Run `kubectl -n hello get policyreports -o wide`. Which objects fail the runAsNonRoot policy, and why?
Optional: add `securityContext:` with `runAsNonRoot: true` to the Pod spec in `k8s/deployment.yaml`, push, and watch the hello-devops result turn to pass.
hints: Artifact attestations are free for public repositories only. On a private repo the attest steps fail, so make the repo public or remove those two steps.
If cosign verify finds no matching signatures, check the identity: your user name, the file name and the tag must match the run exactly.
Redis also fails the runAsNonRoot report. Do not just add the setting: its image starts as root, so the kubelet would refuse to start it. That is why the policy starts in Audit.
task.done_when: `cosign verify` confirms the signature on your 1.2.0 image, and Kyverno rejects the `:latest` Pod.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how your release now protects the supply chain. Mention scanning, signing and the cluster policy.
explain_back.answer: Before anything is pushed, CI scans the image with trivy and stops on serious bugs that have a fix. After the push, it stores an SBOM and signs the image digest with cosign keyless signing. The signature is tied to my release workflow, and there is no key to leak. CI also attaches a signed provenance attestation that says which repo, commit and workflow built the image. In the cluster, Kyverno checks every Pod at admission, so even a hand-made Pod with a :latest image is rejected.

recap: Shift left: put cheap, automatic security checks where code is written and built, and give everything least privilege.
Supply chain attacks hit what you trust; xz-utils, tj-actions and trivy-action are why you pin and verify.
An SBOM lists every package in an image; trivy finds known bugs and risky configuration.
cosign keyless signing ties a signature to your workflow identity, with no private key to leak.
Provenance records how an artifact was built; GitHub attestations reach SLSA Build Level 2.
Kyverno policies check objects at admission: start in Audit, then switch to Deny.

check.q: A new critical bug is announced in a popular Python library. What answers "which of our images contain it?" fastest?
options: The Dockerfile of each service
The SBOMs stored for each release
The cosign signatures of each image
The Kyverno PolicyReports
check.why: An SBOM lists every package and version in each image, so you can search them directly.

check.q: A teammate wants to sign images with a cosign key pair stored as a GitHub secret. What does keyless signing improve?
options: It makes the image smaller to download
It encrypts the image so nobody can read it
It removes the need for a registry
There is no long-lived key to leak or rotate
check.why: Keyless signing uses a short-lived certificate tied to the workflow's OIDC identity, so no private key is stored anywhere.

check.q: You add a policy that blocks Pods without runAsNonRoot, in Deny mode, for all namespaces. What is the most likely problem?
options: New Pods of tools that run as root are blocked too
Kyverno deletes all running Pods at once
Your images stop being signed in CI
Prometheus can no longer scrape any metrics
check.why: An admission policy applies to every new Pod it matches, so start in Audit and scope it to the right namespaces.

interview.q: What is a software supply chain attack, and how do you defend a CI/CD pipeline against one?
interview.a: It is an attack on something you depend on, such as a library, a build tool or a CI action, so that your own build ships the attacker's code. The xz-utils backdoor and the tj-actions/changed-files tag hijack are two recent examples. I pin third-party actions to commit SHAs, keep workflow tokens to least privilege, and use OIDC instead of long-lived keys. I also generate SBOMs, scan images, sign them with provenance, and verify signatures before deploying.

interview.q: What do SBOMs, signatures and provenance each prove?
interview.a: An SBOM lists what is inside an artifact, which helps you find vulnerable packages fast. A signature proves who produced the artifact and that it has not changed since. Provenance says how it was built: which source, commit and build system. SLSA levels describe how far you can trust that record. None of them proves the code is free of bugs; together they make the path from source to running image checkable.

deeper.body:
Signing only helps if something checks the signature. Today you verify by hand with `cosign verify`. The next step is to let the cluster check every Pod.

Kyverno has a policy type for this, ImageValidatingPolicy. You give it:
- Which images it covers, for example `ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/*`.
- Who must have signed them: your release workflow's identity and the GitHub OIDC issuer, as in `cosign verify`.
- Optionally, which attestations must exist, such as SLSA provenance.

When a Pod arrives, Kyverno looks up the signature in the registry and checks it against those rules. An unsigned image, or one signed by another workflow, is rejected. The policy can also replace the tag with the digest it verified, so the node runs exactly the bytes that were checked. Some practical points:
- Kyverno needs network access to the registry and to the Sigstore services.
- Results are cached, but the first check of a new image adds a short delay.
- Start in Audit mode, like any new policy. A typo in the identity would block every deploy.

Kyverno is not the only option. The Sigstore policy-controller is an admission controller made just for cosign signatures, and some managed Kubernetes services have their own image trust features.

Finally, try `trivy config k8s/` on the lab. It flags both Deployments because neither sets a security context, for example: `KSV-0118 (HIGH): deployment hello-devops in hello namespace is using the default security context, which allows root privileges`. The runAsNonRoot policy reports the same gap, only later, at the cluster door. I like having the rule in both places: CI catches it before merge, and the cluster catches whatever skipped CI.

lessons.title: Platform engineering, AI in DevOps, and your capstone
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain platform engineering, FinOps and safe use of AI agents, and ship hello-devops end to end, from a git tag to a signed image that Argo CD runs and Grafana shows.

guess.q: You want an AI agent to help debug your Kubernetes cluster. Which setup is the safest place to start?
options: Give it the admin kubeconfig so it can fix things fast
Let it run any command, but only at night
A read-only identity, with a human reviewing any change
No access at all, and paste logs into a chat forever
guess.why: Read-only access limits what a wrong or tricked agent can break, and a human still approves every change. You keep most of the benefit with little risk.

terms.plain: Building internal tools and services so product teams can ship by themselves, with less to learn.
The self-service tools a platform team offers, such as templates, pipelines and environments.
A supported, ready-made way to do a common task, like creating a new service with CI and monitoring included.
A practice where engineering, finance and the business share responsibility for cloud cost.
An AI tool that can read code, run commands and open pull requests, within limits you set.
Model Context Protocol: an open standard for connecting AI tools to other systems, such as GitHub or Kubernetes.
A limit that stops a person or tool from doing damage, such as read-only access or a required review.

sections.body:
Look at what you built in this course: a Dockerfile, CI, a signed release, Kubernetes YAML, GitOps, dashboards and policies. Now picture 40 product teams each building all of that alone. They would do the same work 40 times, in 40 slightly different ways, and on-call engineers would have to learn every one.

Platform engineering is one answer. A platform team builds an **internal developer platform** and runs it like a product, with developers as its customers. The [CNCF platforms white paper](https://github.com/cncf/tag-app-delivery/blob/main/platforms-whitepaper/latest/index.md) puts self-service at the center: users get what they need without filing a ticket and waiting.

The core idea is the golden path, a supported, ready-made way to do a common job. For example, "create a new service" gives you a repo with a Dockerfile, CI, an Argo CD app and a dashboard, already wired up. Teams may leave the path, but the path is the easy choice.

[Backstage](https://backstage.io/docs/overview/what-is-backstage), a CNCF project, is a popular front door for such a platform. It has:
- A software catalog: every service, its owner and its docs.
- Software templates: golden paths you start from a form.
- TechDocs: documentation written as code, next to the service.

People call the result developer experience. You can measure it in plain terms: how long a new service takes to reach production, and how often a developer has to wait for another team.

refs.title: What is Backstage? (video from the Backstage docs)

sections.body:
In the cloud, any engineer can spend money with one command. FinOps is the practice of making that cost visible and shared between engineering, finance and the business. The [FinOps Foundation](https://www.finops.org/), part of the Linux Foundation, publishes the framework most teams follow. The usual levers, from simple to advanced:
- Visibility: tag cloud resources and label Kubernetes objects with a team, so every cost has an owner.
- Right-sizing: set CPU and memory requests from real usage (Day 18), not guesses.
- Autoscaling: run fewer pods and nodes when traffic is low.
- Turning things off: stop dev environments at night, and destroy what you no longer use (Day 15).
- Spot instances: cheap spare capacity that the provider can take back at short notice, so only for work that can restart.

Start with visibility. Until each cost has an owner, every other lever is a guess. After that, treat cost the way you treat latency: put it on a dashboard, set a target, and look at it every week.

Many teams now use AI tools in daily DevOps work. The common uses:
- Coding agents that take an issue, work on a branch, and open a pull request for review.
- Help in CI: explaining a failed build, suggesting a fix, or reviewing a Terraform plan.
- AI-assisted incident response (AIOps): grouping alerts, summarizing logs and suggesting likely causes.

For example, you can assign an issue to [GitHub Copilot's coding agent](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/using-github-copilot/coding-agent/using-copilot-to-work-on-an-issue). It works on a branch and opens a pull request for you to review. The Claude Code GitHub Action does similar work when you mention it in an issue or pull request.

Most of these tools connect to other systems through the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) (MCP), an open standard. An MCP server wraps one system and offers its actions as tools an agent can call. There are MCP servers for GitHub, for Terraform (from HashiCorp) and for Kubernetes. The agent reads the list of tools and decides which ones to call.

Two risks come with this. An agent can be wrong and sound completely sure. And text it reads, such as a log line or an issue comment, can try to give it orders. This is called prompt injection.

refs.title: GitHub Docs: Copilot coding agent works on an issue

sections.body:
I treat an AI agent like a new contractor on day one: useful, but it does not get the keys yet. The guardrails:
- Read-only by default. The GitHub MCP server, for example, has a `--read-only` flag.
- Least privilege: the agent gets its own identity with narrow rights, never production admin keys.
- Short-lived credentials: a token that expires in an hour limits the damage of a leak.
- Human review: the agent proposes a pull request or a `terraform plan`, and a person approves it.
- Untrusted input: everything the agent reads is data, never instructions.

The other two MCP servers have similar switches. The Kubernetes MCP server has a read-only setting. The Terraform MCP server keeps the tools that need approval switched off unless you enable them.

Over-scoped credentials are an old problem, and AI tools raise the stakes. In July 2025, [AWS reported](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-015/) that an attacker used a GitHub token with too much scope. With it, the attacker put malicious code into a release of the Amazon Q Developer extension for VS Code. The worked example below sets up the narrow, short-lived access these rules ask for.

sections.h: Other trends worth a line each
sections.body:
You will hear these names in job ads and talks:
- eBPF runs small, safe programs inside the Linux kernel. [Cilium](https://github.com/cilium/cilium) uses it for Kubernetes networking and can replace kube-proxy.
- OpenTofu is the open source fork of Terraform under the Linux Foundation (Day 13). The commands are nearly the same.
- Serverless containers (AWS Fargate, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps) run your image with no servers or cluster to manage.
- WebAssembly (Wasm) runs small, sandboxed programs that start very fast, at the edge or as plugins inside other tools.

sections.h: Careers, certifications and what to learn next
sections.body:
The roles from Day 1 all use what you learned: DevOps engineer, site reliability engineer (SRE) and platform engineer. A certification gives your learning a shape and a deadline. Your hello-devops repo shows what you can actually do. Good next steps, roughly in this order:
- KCNA (Kubernetes and Cloud Native Associate), from the Linux Foundation and CNCF: multiple choice and broad.
- CKAD (Certified Kubernetes Application Developer): a hands-on exam in a real terminal, about running apps.
- CKA (Certified Kubernetes Administrator): hands-on as well, about running clusters.
- HashiCorp Certified: Terraform Associate. The current exam version is 004.
- AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner: cloud basics, billing and core services on AWS.
- The GitHub Actions certification (exam GH-200), offered by GitHub through Microsoft Learn.

After the capstone, I would do four things. Deploy hello-devops to one managed Kubernetes service. Add tracing with OpenTelemetry. Write one alert on an SLO. Then read the [Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/), which is free online. And keep shipping small changes to a real project.

worked.title: Give an AI agent a read-only key to your cluster

steps.say: Say you want to try an MCP server for Kubernetes. Do not hand it your own kubeconfig: on kind, that is full admin. Create a separate identity with the built-in `view` role in one namespace instead. The file is `policy/ai-agent-readonly.yaml` in Files.
steps.code:
$ kubectl apply -f policy/ai-agent-readonly.yaml
serviceaccount/ai-agent created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/ai-agent-view created

steps.say: Ask the API server what this identity may do, before you use it. `--as` acts as that identity for one question. Listing pods in `hello` is allowed.
steps.code:
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:ai-agent
yes

steps.say: Deleting is not allowed, Secrets are hidden, and other namespaces are closed. The `view` role leaves out Secrets on purpose, because they hold passwords and tokens.
steps.code:
$ kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:ai-agent
no
$ kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:ai-agent
no
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:ai-agent
no

steps.say: Create a token that expires in one hour and a separate kubeconfig context that uses only that token. Your kind cluster is called `kind-devops` in kubeconfig.
steps.code:
$ TOKEN=$(kubectl -n hello create token ai-agent --duration=1h)
$ kubectl config set-credentials ai-agent --token="$TOKEN"
User "ai-agent" set.
$ kubectl config set-context ai-agent --cluster=kind-devops --user=ai-agent --namespace=hello
Context "ai-agent" created.

steps.say: Try it. Reading works. The API server refuses the delete, whatever the agent was told to do.
steps.code:
$ kubectl --context ai-agent get deploy
NAME           READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
hello-devops   3/3     3            3           2d
redis          1/1     1            1           2d
$ kubectl --context ai-agent delete deploy redis
Error from server (Forbidden): deployments.apps "redis" is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:hello:ai-agent" cannot delete resource "deployments" in API group "apps" in the namespace "hello"

steps.say: An MCP server, or any other tool, can now use the `ai-agent` context. If the agent finds a fix, it proposes a pull request, and Argo CD applies it after a human merges it. Remove the test context when you are done.
steps.code:
$ kubectl config delete-context ai-agent
$ kubectl config delete-user ai-agent

code.title: policy/ai-agent-readonly.yaml
code.src:
# A read-only identity for an AI agent (or any helper tool) in namespace hello.
# It can look (get, list, watch) but not change anything, and it cannot read Secrets.
# Apply:      kubectl apply -f policy/ai-agent-readonly.yaml
# Get token:  kubectl -n hello create token ai-agent --duration=1h
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: ai-agent
  namespace: hello
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: ai-agent-view
  namespace: hello
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: ai-agent
    namespace: hello
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: view # built in: read most things in the namespace, but not Secrets

    newTag: 1.2.0
